prompt: I found an off-by-one error in the open-source CSV parser we rely on at Acme Corp while processing large datasets last week. The bug causes the last column to be dropped when a row ends with a delimiter. I have already fixed this in a local branch and verified it against our internal data. However, the upstream project has a strict rule that all contributions must include a new test case demonstrating the failure before the fix. I am worried about writing a test that fits their existing style without breaking their custom test runner. I need you to draft a minimal test case file that reproduces this specific edge case using their current testing patterns, so I can attach it to my pull request immediately.

Our team at Northwind Logistics needs a retry option for the popular HTTP client we use, as our external API calls often fail due to transient network issues. I have designed the feature and implemented a prototype, but the project maintainers explicitly state in their contributing guide that no code will be reviewed unless a corresponding issue exists first to discuss the design. I have not opened an issue yet because I am unsure how to frame the proposal to match their architectural preferences. Please write a detailed issue description that outlines the problem, proposes the retry mechanism, and anticipates potential concerns about backward compatibility, so I can submit it to the tracker today.

While working in our private monorepo at Globex, we discovered a custom lint rule that effectively catches a common race condition in async functions. I believe this logic would benefit the wider community if added to the open-source linter we all use. I have extracted the core logic and adapted it to the public codebase, but the project requires that any new rule include comprehensive documentation explaining the error pattern and how to disable it if needed. I am constrained by time and cannot write clear, user-facing docs that match their tone. Could you generate a documentation draft for this new rule, including code examples of both the bad pattern and the corrected version, ready for their docs folder?

I noticed a typo and a misleading code example on the documentation site for a library I use daily. This would be my very first open-source contribution, and I want to make sure I do not mess up the process. The project uses a static site generator where every page has a specific front-matter header that must include an author tag and a last-reviewed date, or the build fails. I have fixed the text and the code snippet, but I am anxious about formatting the header correctly since I have never touched this system before. Please provide a checklist of steps to verify my changes locally, including exactly how to update the front-matter so the automated build does not reject my pull request.

I have completed a massive 900-line refactor in my fork of a utility library to fix a deep-seated memory leak that affects our services at Initech. The fix works perfectly, but the upstream maintainers are known to reject large pull requests and strictly prefer incremental changes split across multiple smaller submissions. I am unsure how to break down this monolithic change without losing the context of the overall fix or introducing intermediate broken states. I need a concrete plan that divides this work into four or five logical, mergeable pull requests, describing what each one should contain and in what order they must be submitted to ensure the repository remains stable throughout the process.

I am preparing a contribution to a project hosted by Hooli that recently updated its contributing guide to require explicit disclosure if any part of the code was generated or assisted by an AI tool. I used an AI assistant to help generate the boilerplate for my new module, although I wrote all the business logic myself. The guide states that failing to disclose this will result in an immediate closure of the pull request. I am worried that my disclosure statement might be too vague or too verbose. Please draft a concise and honest disclosure paragraph that I can add to my pull request description, clearly stating the extent of AI assistance while affirming my ownership of the final implementation.

I developed a fix for a connection timeout bug against our company's internal service at Umbrella Corp, and I want to upstream this improvement to the public version of the library. The problem is that my local test fixtures still contain hardcoded internal hostnames and IP addresses that cannot be exposed publicly. The project rules forbid any internal infrastructure details in the codebase, and I must sanitize these before submitting. I need you to review my test fixture file and replace all internal references with generic, safe placeholders that still allow the tests to run logically, ensuring no sensitive data leaks while maintaining the validity of the test scenarios.

My pull request for a simple configuration update is currently blocked because a flaky CI test failed, which is completely unrelated to the files I touched. The maintainers have a policy that they will not review any PR with a red CI status, even if the failure is known to be intermittent. I cannot rerun the full suite myself due to permission limits on the repository. I need a polite and factual comment to post on the pull request that explains the situation, links to the known issue tracker for the flaky test, and requests a maintainer to trigger a re-run, without sounding like I am making excuses for the failure.

The maintainer of the project has requested specific changes to my pull request, and simultaneously, three different bots have left automated comments about formatting, commit message style, and missing changelog entries. I need to rebase my branch to address the human feedback while also satisfying all the bot requirements to clear the checks. The project rules state that pushing new commits without rebasing first will clutter the history and lead to rejection. I am overwhelmed by the number of constraints. Please provide a step-by-step command sequence to rebase my branch, amend the commits to fix the bot issues, and push the updates safely, ensuring I do not lose the maintainer's context or break the branch history.

I only ran a subset of the tests locally due to hardware limitations on my development machine, specifically skipping the heavy integration suite that requires a dedicated database cluster. The project requires that the pull request description explicitly confirm that all tests pass before a review begins, but I cannot verify the full suite myself. I am worried that stating "all tests pass" would be dishonest, yet leaving it blank might cause the PR to be ignored. Please draft a precise sentence for my pull request description that accurately reflects my local testing scope, acknowledges the skipped suite, and politely asks the maintainers or the CI system to verify the full test run upon submission.

I recently solved a recurring problem in our internal Acme project where our automation agents kept misinterpreting context variables. The fix was a specific prompt pattern that forces the agent to validate inputs before acting. I want to contribute this pattern to the public Northwind Agent Config repository so others can benefit. I have drafted the documentation, but it currently includes references to our private client data and internal server names which must be removed. The project maintainers are very strict about leaking any proprietary information, even accidentally, and will reject any pull request containing such details immediately. I need you to review my draft text and produce a sanitized version that explains the pattern clearly using only fictional examples like "Widget Corp" or "Test User," ensuring no trace of our actual infrastructure remains while keeping the technical logic intact.

While auditing the dependencies for our Horizon Logistics dashboard, I noticed that the widely used "SafeParse" library, which handles all our input validation, might have a critical security vulnerability involving recursive object parsing. I found a discussion on a security forum suggesting that specially crafted payloads could cause a denial of service, but there is no official advisory yet. I have created a minimal reproduction case in a private branch that demonstrates the crash under load. However, the upstream project has a strict policy against publishing unverified security flaws in public issues to prevent exploitation before a patch exists. I am worried about violating this rule while trying to get attention. Please generate a secure, encrypted message template I can send directly to the lead maintainer, Jane Doe, describing the issue and attaching my reproduction steps without exposing the vulnerability details publicly.

I am working on a new feature for the Stellar Desktop GUI application that allows users to export reports to a custom isolated data directory. The implementation is complete in my local fork, and the code follows the existing architecture patterns. To get this merged into the main Galaxy UI repository, the contribution guidelines explicitly require before-and-after screenshots showing the new file picker dialog in action, as well as a verification that the app correctly handles permission errors on read-only folders. I do not have access to a Windows testing environment, which is where most of our users operate, and I cannot generate these images myself. I need you to create a detailed checklist of exactly which UI states I must capture and what specific error conditions I need to simulate, so I can ask a colleague with the right setup to generate the assets for me efficiently.

I submitted a bug fix to the OpenTrack inventory system three weeks ago regarding a race condition that causes duplicate order entries during high traffic. The pull request includes a comprehensive test suite and passes all continuous integration checks, but there has been absolutely no response from the maintainers. The project documentation states that issues older than fourteen days without activity may be closed automatically by a bot to keep the queue clean, and I am terrified my work will be lost before anyone reviews it. I have already commented once politely asking for feedback, but I do not want to seem pushy or spammy. Please draft a concise, professional follow-up message I can post on the pull request that highlights the urgency of the bug for production users and politely requests a preliminary review or an estimate of when the team might look at it.

I am a contributor to the Flux Network monitoring tool, and we have an urgent production incident where the current logging format is breaking our downstream analytics pipeline. I have write access to the upstream repository via an automated bot token used for emergency hotfixes. My instinct is to push the fix directly to the main branch to resolve the outage immediately. However, the project governance document strictly forbids direct pushes to main, even for emergencies, requiring all changes to go through a pull request with at least one human approval to maintain an audit trail. I am under immense pressure from my manager at Vertex Systems to fix this within the hour. Please outline a rapid but compliant workflow that allows me to open a pull request, tag the specific on-call maintainer for immediate review, and merge the fix as quickly as possible without violating the no-direct-push rule.

Last month, our team at Nebula Cloud experienced a severe outage because a deployment action failed to verify the integrity of the artifact checksum before promoting it to production. We conducted a private postmortem and identified that a specific validation step was missing in the open-source deploy action we all use. I want to contribute this lesson back to the community by adding the missing check to the official "DeployMaster" action repository. I have written the code based on our internal fix, but I must ensure that no specific details about our outage, such as timestamps, affected services, or internal IP addresses, are included in the commit message or code comments. The project maintainers reject any contribution that looks like it references a specific company incident. Please review my proposed commit message and rewrite it to describe the general class of error and the fix abstractly, ensuring it serves as a universal lesson rather than a specific incident report.

I am attempting to add full Japanese language support to the GlobalChat open-source project. I have translated all the user-facing strings and verified the content with a native speaker. The project has extremely strict formatting rules for localization files: keys must be sorted alphabetically, no trailing commas are allowed, and every string must end with a specific newline character sequence. My local tests pass, but the automated linter in the continuous integration pipeline keeps rejecting my pull request due to minor whitespace inconsistencies that are invisible in my editor. I am running out of patience trying to manually fix these formatting errors. Please provide a step-by-step plan or a script logic description that I can run locally to automatically reformat my translation file to match the project's exact specifications, ensuring the next pull request I submit passes the linter checks on the first try.

I have developed a performance optimization for the RiverData processing engine that reduces memory usage by thirty percent during large batch operations. The code is ready, tested, and pushed to my fork. Before I can open a pull request to the upstream repository, I noticed that the project requires every contributor to sign a Contributor Licence Agreement and include a specific "Signed-off-by" trailer in every single commit message. I have never contributed to a project with these legal requirements before, and I am unsure if I need to sign the document before creating the pull request or if I can do it during the review process. Additionally, I am worried that my existing commits lack the required sign-off trailer. Please generate a clear checklist of the exact legal and git steps I must complete, including how to amend my existing commits to include the necessary sign-off lines without losing my change history.

I am proposing a change to the ConfigLite library that alters how environment variables override configuration files. Currently, the system merges them recursively, which causes unexpected behavior when nested keys share names. My fix changes this to a shallow merge, which breaks backward compatibility for a small subset of users relying on the old deep merge behavior. The project maintainers have a rigid policy that any backward-incompatible change must include a detailed entry in the changelog explaining the migration path for affected users, and the pull request will be rejected without it. I have the code ready, but I am struggling to articulate the breaking change clearly and provide a helpful migration guide. Please draft a changelog entry that clearly explains the behavior change, identifies who is affected, and provides a concrete code example showing how users should update their configuration to achieve the same result under the new logic.

I fixed a crash in the AeroMap rendering engine that occurs when loading vector tiles with missing geometry attributes. I spent several hours debugging this and finally implemented a guard clause to handle the null values gracefully. Before I spend time writing tests and formatting the code for a pull request, I have a strong suspicion that this issue might have already been reported or even fixed in a recent merge that I missed, as the issue tracker is quite active. I do not want to waste the maintainers' time with a duplicate contribution. Please help me formulate a precise search query and a strategy to check the recent commit history and open issues for keywords related to "vector tile crash" and "null geometry," so I can confirm whether my fix is novel or if I should simply update an existing ticket instead of creating a new pull request.
